what: Plains GP Holdings is the vehicle through which investors own a share of Plains All American, a large crude oil pipeline and storage business. Plains gathers crude from the Permian Basin and other producing regions, moves it by pipeline, stores it in tank farms and markets it, and also handles natural gas liquids in Canada.
customers: Oil producers who need to move barrels from the wellhead to market, and refiners and exporters who need them delivered. Pipeline capacity is sold under contracts, and the marketing arm buys and resells physical crude.
money: Gathering, pipeline transportation, terminalling and storage, plus physical crude marketing.
Processing, fractionation and marketing of NGLs, mostly in Canada.
moat: Pipelines connected to specific wells and refineries are effectively irreplaceable: nobody is permitting a new crude line across Texas. Plains owns the gathering systems that collect Permian barrels at the wellhead, which is the part of the chain closest to the producer and the hardest to bypass. Growing Permian production has to travel on someone’s pipe, and Plains owns a lot of it.
risks: Reported revenue of about $55.9B is mostly the marketing business buying and reselling physical crude, so it bears no relation to earning power: net income is $539.0M on that figure.
Debt is about $11.5B against $329.0M of cash, high even by midstream standards.
Volumes depend on Permian production growth, which depends on the oil price and on producers’ capital discipline.
The structure is complicated: this entity owns an interest in a partnership, which affects tax treatment and makes the accounts harder to read than an ordinary company’s.
Thirteen analysts average a $26.85 target against a $25.87 price, implying almost no upside.
opportunities: Free cash flow of about $2.3B against a $6.0B market value is a very large yield, and the shares trade at about 2.7 times free cash flow and 5.8 times EV/EBITDA.
Fee-based pipeline contracts insulate much of the earnings from the oil price, unlike a producer.
Permian production has continued to grow, and every additional barrel needs gathering and transport.
The distribution is the main reason to hold this, and the cash flow covers it with room to spare.
watch: Permian volumes on the system, and the share of earnings that is fee-based rather than from marketing. The marketing business is volatile and low quality; the pipeline fees are what the distribution should be judged against.
view: The first thing to do with Plains is throw away the revenue line. Fifty-six billion dollars of revenue against $539 million of net income is not a one-percent-margin business; it is an accounting artifact of the marketing arm, which buys and resells physical crude and books the gross value of both sides. Judge this company on EV/EBITDA, on free cash flow and on the share of earnings that comes from pipeline fees rather than from trading. On those measures — 5.8 times EV/EBITDA, $2.3 billion of free cash flow against a $6.0 billion market value — it looks like what it is: a cheap, cash-generative toll road.

The asset quality is genuinely good in one specific way that gets underrated. Plains owns gathering systems, the small pipes that collect barrels at the wellhead in the Permian, not just the long-haul lines. Gathering is the stickiest part of the chain: it is physically connected to specific well pads and there is no second pipe. Long-haul capacity faces competition and occasional overbuild; gathering does not. As long as the Permian produces, those barrels travel on somebody’s gathering system, and Plains has a lot of them.

Against that sit two things. The $11.5 billion of debt is high even for midstream, where leverage is normal, and it means a meaningful share of the cash flow is spoken for before shareholders see any. And the structure is genuinely awkward: this entity holds an interest in a partnership, the tax treatment differs from an ordinary share, and anyone buying it should understand what they will receive and how it is taxed before they buy it rather than after.

The thirteen analysts seeing essentially no upside are, I think, roughly right about the share price and beside the point about the investment. You do not buy a midstream company for capital appreciation; you buy it for the distribution and the durability of the cash flow behind it. On that basis the question is narrow: what share of earnings is contracted pipeline fees rather than marketing profit, and is Permian volume still growing. If the answer to both is favourable, this is a reasonable income holding at a cheap multiple. It is not, and was never going to be, a growth story.
bull: Permian volumes keep growing through gathering systems nobody can bypass, fee-based earnings cover the distribution comfortably, and debt comes down against a 2.7 times free cash flow multiple.
bear: Permian growth stalls with the oil price, marketing earnings swing the wrong way, and $11.5 billion of debt leaves little room between the cash flow and the distribution.
